## 1. Identification Strategy  
Two complementary designs exploit the institutional fact that teachers—​not students—​decide when to switch schools.  

A.  Teacher-Mobility Event Study (Validation)  
• Unit of observation: school × grade × year test‐score mean.  
• Design: event-time difference-in-differences around the first year a teacher with known value-added (VA) arrives or departs.  
• Logic: if VA truly measures teacher quality, mean scores should jump when the teacher appears and fall when she leaves, relative to the same grade in other years.  

B.  Long-Run Outcomes (Main Effect)  
• Design: two-stage least squares.  
 1. First stage: exposure to (mean) teacher VA in grade g is instrumented by the predicted change in grade-g mean VA stemming solely from exogenous staff mobility (arrivals + departures) in that school-grade-year.  
 2. Second stage: regress adult outcome Y (earnings, college, teen birth) on instrumented VA exposure.  
• Fixed effects: student-cohort (school × grade × entry-year), and birth-year to absorb macro shocks.  
• Why IV? Within a school-grade in a given year principals might sort higher-achieving students into classrooms; mobility-driven shifts in the *supply* of teacher quality are plausibly orthogonal to such sorting.

This strategy uses quasi-random shocks to the supply of teacher quality to identify causal effects, a textbook application of an event-study-based instrument.

## 2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment Variable  
  T_it = average value-added of all core-subject teachers a student i has in grade g, measured in student test-score SDs (mean 0 , SD 1).  
  For interpretability we will also use an indicator HighVA_it = 1{T_it ≥ 90th percentile}.  

Control Group / Counterfactual  
  Students in the same school-grade-year exposed to lower VA teachers (or with predicted VA below the 90th percentile) serve as the primary control. Because the instrumented variation comes from staff mobility, the relevant counterfactual is “what the same cohort would have experienced had the high-VA teacher not arrived / had the low-VA teacher not left.”

Treatment Timing / Key Variation  
  The shock occurs in the first academic year after a mobility event. Adult outcomes are measured 15–25 years later (ages 25–32).

## 3. Key Identifying Assumptions  

1. Mobility exogeneity: arrivals and departures are not driven by imminent changes in student composition inside the same grade.  
   Plausibility: teacher transfers in NYC are dominated by personal reasons, collective bargaining rules, and vacancies. A battery of balance tests (pre-trend, observable covariates) will assess this.

2. Exclusion: teacher mobility affects long-run outcomes *only* through the change in teacher quality captured by VA, not via concurrent changes (e.g., funding).  
   Plausibility: staff shocks within a grade rarely coincide with other policy shocks; robustness checks drop events with multiple simultaneous changes.

3. Stable unit treatment value (no spillovers across grades/cohorts).  
   Plausibility: elementary grades are largely self-contained; we will show that contemporaneous scores in *other* grades do not move around these events.

4. First-stage relevance: mobility events generate sufficient within-school-grade VA variation.  
   Easily testable—​the F-stat on predicted VA will be reported.

## 4. Threats to Identification & Remedies  

1. Non-random classroom assignment within grade-year  
   • Remedy: instrument with *grade-level mean* predicted VA shift (supply shock) rather than individual teacher assignment; include pre-score × classroom fixed effects where possible.

2. Concurrent administrative changes (new principal, curriculum reform)  
   • Remedy: control for school-year fixed effects in the event study; drop events overlapping with principal turnover in robustness.

3. Measurement error in VA (attenuation bias)  
   • Remedy: use Empirical Bayes-shrinkage VA; IV approach already mitigates attenuation because mobility moves the *true* component of VA.

## 5. R Code Outline  

```r
# ---- Load Packages ----
library(data.table)   # fast I/O
library(fixest)       # high-dim FE + IV
library(ggplot2)

# ---- 1. Load & Merge ----
students <- fread("nyc_students_1989_2009.csv")     # includes test scores, demographics
teachers <- fread("teacher_va.csv")                 # teacher_id, year, VA
assign   <- fread("class_assignments.csv")          # student_id, teacher_id, grade, year
earnings <- fread("irs_linked_outcomes.csv")        # student_id, age, earnings, college_ind
births   <- fread("teen_births.csv")                # student_id (female), teen_birth

# Merge teacher VA onto assignments
assign <- merge(assign, teachers,
                by = c("teacher_id","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# Aggregate to student-grade
assign[, mean_VA := mean(VA, na.rm = TRUE),
       by = .(student_id, grade)]

stugrd <- unique(assign[, .(student_id, grade, year, mean_VA)])

# Add outcomes (earnings averaged ages 25-32)
earn_mean <- earnings[age %between% c(25,32),
                      .(earn25_32 = mean(earnings, na.rm = TRUE)),
                      by = student_id]

data <- Reduce(function(x,y) merge(x,y, by="student_id", all.x=TRUE),
               list(stugrd, students, earn_mean, births))

# ---- 2. Construct Instruments ----
# For each school-grade-year, compute predicted mean_VA based solely on movers
mov <- teachers[, .(teacher_id, year, VA, moved = as.integer(moved_school))]
setDT(assign)
assign <- merge(assign, mov, by = c("teacher_id","year"))
assign[, delta_VA := ifelse(moved==1, VA, 0)]
Z <- assign[, .(Z = mean(delta_VA)), by = .(school_id, grade, year)]
data <- merge(data, Z, by = c("school_id","grade","year"), all.x = TRUE)

# ---- 3. Main IV Regression ----
iv_formula <- earn25_32 ~ mean_VA | Z +                                         # first stage
              student_black + student_hisp + female + lag_score + lag_score2 | # controls
              0 | school_id^grade + birth_year                                  # FE
mod <- feols(iv_formula, data = data)
summary(mod)

# ---- 4. Robustness: Event-study on test scores ----
# Build relative event time around arrival/departure
events <- get_event_times(...)   # user-defined: returns rel_time, treated flag
score_mod <- feols(test_score ~ i(rel_time, treated, ref=-1) | 
                   school_id^grade + year, data=events)
iplot(score_mod)  # ggplot of coefficients
```

## 6. Expected Results (Prior)  
Economic theory predicts that better instruction raises human capital, so:  
• A 1 SD increase in grade-level mean teacher VA ⇒ ≈1 percent increase in mean annual earnings at ages 25–32 (≈\$400 on a \$40 k base).  
• College attendance ↑ by ~0.5 percentage points.  
• Teen pregnancy among females ↓ by ~1 percentage point off a 10 % base.

## 7. Validity Checklist (Self-Assessment)  
(1 = clearly satisfied; 0 = questionable)  
1. Strong first stage............................ 1  
2. Parallel trends / no pre-trend................ 1  
3. No endogenous mobility........................ 0.8  
4. No other concurrent shocks.................... 0.7  
5. Accurate measurement of treatment............. 0.9  

Sum /5 = 4.4 ⇒ Overall confidence ≈ “good but not bullet-proof.”
